podcast.body: This song became the subject of a famous sampling lawsuit. It used a six-second string figure from the 1966 Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra version of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time," arranged by David Whitaker. The Verve initially cleared rights with Decca Records, but not with Abko Records, owned by Allan Klein, who held rights to earlier Stones material. Klein sued, leading Richard Ashcroft to sign over all songwriting credits and rights to the entire song to Klein, who credited Jagger/Richards. Ashcroft received only $1,000 and no royalties from 1997 until May 2019, when the rights were returned after Klein's death. "But one of the most famous sampling lawsuits involves the Verve, and how they lost control of their song, Bittersweet Symphony for decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Written by Richard Ashcroft, this song was inspired by a five-note progression from Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra's 1965 cover of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." The Verve initially licensed the snippet from Abkco Music (controlled by Allen Klein) for 50% of the song's earnings. However, Abkco later sued, claiming more of the sample was used than agreed, and Andrew Loog Oldham also sued for $1.7 million in royalties. Under duress, The Verve surrendered 100% of the publishing to Abkco and Oldham, leading to the songwriting credits being changed to "Ashcroft Jagger Richards." Abkco subsequently licensed the recording to Nike for a TV commercial, which was seen as "selling out" and severely damaged the band's artistic integrity with their indie fanbase, despite it not being their decision. The song was nominated for a Grammy, with the songwriters listed as "Jagger Richards," and the original five-note bit was actually written by orchestral arranger David Whitaker. "Richard Ashcroft of the Verve came up with a song called Bittersweet Symphony."

podcast.body: This song is noted as the only track from The Verve to ever make it into the Billboard Hot 100 Top 40, leading to the band being categorized as a one-hit wonder by a strict chart definition. However, this categorization overlooks the band's broader catalog of acclaimed songs. "Bittersweet Symphony, which is the only song from the band ever to make it into the Billboard Hot 100 Top 40."
